sections.h2: What notice does a Florida landlord have to give before filing an eviction?
sections.html:
The notice depends on why the landlord wants the tenant out, and Florida law sets a different clock for each reason. Missed rent starts a three day clock, a lease breach starts a seven day clock, and a tenancy with no fixed end needs a longer warning before the rental period closes.

A notice is the step that comes before any court filing. A landlord who skips it, or serves one with the wrong number of days, gives the tenant a defense. Owners planning to sell a rented house should sort out the notice first, because a buyer will ask whether the home comes vacant.

The rules sit in Chapter 83 of the Florida Statutes, the residential landlord and tenant chapter. The sections cited below are on the Legislature's website, and the notice itself should follow the wording of the section that fits the facts.

sections.h2: How does the three day notice for unpaid rent work?
sections.html:
Under section 83.56(3), the landlord delivers a written notice that gives the tenant three days to pay or leave. The count leaves out Saturdays, Sundays and court observed legal holidays.

That exclusion matters. A notice handed over on a Friday does not run out on Monday, and a holiday week stretches the period again. Landlords who count calendar days tend to file early, and an early filing is a weak one.

  • The notice must demand either payment of the rent or possession of the unit.
  • It has to be in writing, and the lease cannot waive the notice requirement.
  • If the landlord takes partial rent after serving it, the landlord must give a receipt that shows the balance due, pay the partial rent into the court registry when filing, or serve a fresh three day notice.

The partial payment rule catches many small owners. Taking a check for half the rent and then filing on the original notice can undo the whole case.

sections.h2: What happens when a tenant breaks the lease in some way other than rent?
sections.html:
The statute splits lease violations into those the tenant can fix and those the tenant cannot. A curable violation gives the tenant seven days after delivery to cure it. An incurable one, such as intentional damage to the property or a repeated unreasonable disturbance, gives the tenant seven days to vacate.

If the same violation comes back within twelve months, the landlord may sue without serving a new notice. Records of earlier notices are worth keeping in the file for that reason.

A notice for a curable breach should name the breach and say what the tenant must do within the seven days. A vague notice invites an argument that the tenant never knew what to fix.

sections.h2: How must the notice be delivered?
sections.html:
Delivery under the same section can be by mail, by handing the tenant a true copy, by email under section 83.505, or by leaving a copy at the residence when the tenant is away. A landlord should keep proof of whichever method was used.

The lease cannot waive the notice rules. A clause that says the tenant gives up notice, or that shortens the period, does not bind the tenant under the statute. Check the lease anyway, since it may set the place where notices go or the amount of rent that is due.

  • Date the notice and keep a copy.
  • Record who delivered it, how, and when.
  • Calendar the end of the count, skipping weekends and legal holidays for the rent notice.

sections.h2: How long does a landlord have to give when there is no lease end date?
sections.html:
A tenancy that rolls from period to period ends with a notice that matches the period, and section 83.57 gives the lengths. The notice has to come before the end of the rental period.

Notice for ending a periodic tenancy, as printed in section 83.57
Type of tenancyNotice before the period ends
Year to yearNot less than 60 days
Quarter to quarterNot less than 30 days
Month to monthNot less than 30 days
Week to weekNot less than 7 days

A month to month tenant is the common case for a single family rental. The landlord who wants the house empty for a sale can use this route when the tenant has done nothing wrong, as long as the notice is served in time for the period to end on schedule.

sections.h2: What records should a landlord keep for a notice?
sections.html:
A short paper trail protects the case if the tenant contests the notice. The file should show what was served, to whom, how, and when the count began.

  • A copy of the notice exactly as delivered, with the address of the rental.
  • Proof of delivery: a mailing receipt, a note of the person who handed it over, or the email record where section 83.505 allows email.
  • A rent ledger showing what was owed on the day the notice went out.
  • Any receipt given for partial rent taken afterward.

These records also help at a sale. A title company reviewing an occupied rental will want to see that any earlier notice was valid and that no step was left half done.

sections.h2: What comes after the notice expires?
sections.html:
The landlord has to file a complaint in county court, and the sheriff, not the landlord, removes a tenant who stays. Locking out a tenant or removing belongings without a court order is not part of the process.

A tenant who answers with a defense other than payment must put the accrued rent into the court registry, or file a motion to determine rent, within five days after service. Weekends and legal holidays do not count in that five days. A tenant who does not do this waives the defenses, and the landlord can ask for a default judgment right away, under section 83.60(2).

After a judgment for the landlord, the clerk issues a writ to the sheriff. The sheriff posts a 24 hour notice and then puts the landlord back in possession, and weekends and holidays do not pause those 24 hours under section 83.62.

sections.h2: How does an eviction notice affect selling the house?
sections.html:
An occupied rental can be sold, but the notice period and the court calendar control when a buyer can get keys. Owners who need a firm closing date should decide early whether to sell with the tenant in place or deliver the home vacant.

The choices usually come down to these:

  • Sell with the tenant in place and let the buyer take over the lease.
  • End a periodic tenancy with the proper notice, then list the home empty.
  • Serve a rent or breach notice if the tenant is in default, and wait out the court steps.

Whatever the route, the notice must be valid first. A buyer or title company that sees an unfinished eviction may delay the closing until the occupant is gone. For legal advice on a specific notice, speak with a Florida attorney or the clerk of the county court where the rental sits.

faqs.q: How many days is a Florida eviction notice for unpaid rent?
faqs.a: Three days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and court observed legal holidays. The notice must demand either the rent or possession of the unit, and it must be in writing.

faqs.q: Can a Florida landlord evict without a notice?
faqs.a: No. The notice comes first, and a missing or defective one gives the tenant a defense. The lease cannot waive the notice requirement, so a clause saying otherwise has no force under the statute.

faqs.q: How much notice ends a month to month tenancy in Florida?
faqs.a: At least 30 days before the end of a monthly period. Year to year tenancies need 60 days, quarter to quarter 30 days, and week to week 7 days.

faqs.q: What if the tenant violates the lease but pays rent?
faqs.a: The landlord serves a seven day notice. If the violation can be fixed, the tenant gets seven days to cure it. If it cannot, such as intentional damage, the tenant gets seven days to vacate.

faqs.q: Who removes a tenant after the court rules for the landlord?
faqs.a: The sheriff does. The clerk issues a writ, and the sheriff posts a 24 hour notice before returning possession to the landlord. Weekends and holidays do not stop that 24 hours.
